title: Portrait of Ihaka Whanga
altText: A painted portrait of a man named Ihaka Whanga, with the figure as the main focus of the canvas. It is a formal oil portrait made to show the sitter with dignity.

source.verifiedBy: arthistoryproject.com artwork page text (title, year, medium, collection, public-domain statement)

context: An oil painting made in 1870 by Gottfried Lindauer, a painter who worked in New Zealand and made many portraits of Maori sitters. The source page tags it Portraits. The sitter is named in the title, so he is remembered as a person with a name and a story.

descriptions.k: This is a painted picture of a man named Ihaka Whanga. Look at his face. Look at what he wears. How do you think he feels? What would you like to ask him?
descriptions.g12: Gottfried Lindauer painted this portrait of Ihaka Whanga in New Zealand. A portrait is a picture of a real person. Look at his face, his clothing, and how he sits or stands. What do these tell you about him?
descriptions.g35: Gottfried Lindauer painted Portrait of Ihaka Whanga in 1870 in New Zealand. A portrait shows a real person, and the title tells us his name. Look closely at the face, the clothing, and the pose. What clues help you imagine his character, and what would you still like to find out?
descriptions.g68: Lindauer's Portrait of Ihaka Whanga (1870) presents a named individual in oil paint. Naming the sitter matters: it treats him as a person with his own life and place in his community. Consider how the face, clothing, and pose are shown. What do they suggest, and what do you still need to learn from the sitter's own people and history?
descriptions.g910: Portrait of Ihaka Whanga (1870) is an oil portrait by Gottfried Lindauer, who worked in New Zealand and painted many Maori sitters. A portrait balances likeness with the choices of the painter and the wishes of the subject. How do pose, dress, and setting shape the dignity of the sitter, and whose perspective is missing when we look only at the painting?
descriptions.g1112: Lindauer's Portrait of Ihaka Whanga (1870) raises questions central to portraiture in colonial settings: who made the image, for whom, and how the sitter wished to be seen. A European-trained painter working in New Zealand records a named individual in oil. How might the portrait be read as a likeness, a cultural record, or a product of its time, and what voices should shape that reading?

safety.method: Image viewed and approved by the site owner (visual review) on 2026-10-18. Earlier metadata screening: Title, medium and page tag (Portraits) read from the arthistoryproject.com page; no concerning terms. Only page text was read. The image itself was not visually inspected; a person should confirm it before release, ideally with consideration for the sitter's community and respectful presentation of the portrait.

teacherNote.context: An 1870 oil portrait by Gottfried Lindauer, who worked in New Zealand. The sitter, Ihaka Whanga, is named in the title. Teachers may wish to invite local or Maori community voices to add context.
directions: Ask students to list what a portrait can tell us and what it cannot.
Discuss why it matters that the sitter is named in the title.
Invite students to research the sitter's community using respectful, reliable sources such as the Auckland Art Gallery.
